newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania, with new government, appeals for calm.
newsitem.headline: Albania, with new government, appeals for calm.

text.p: Albanian authorities, buoyed by a new all-party government, appealed for calm amid fresh reports of looting of arms and an unyielding campaign by rebels demanding the resignation of President Sali Berisha.

The United States, prompted by what it said was deteriorating security, ordered 160 government employees to leave the country along with their families. A European mediation team led by former Austrian leader Franz Vranitzky was due in Tirana on Thursday in a new bid to end the revolt.

Albania's "government of national reconciliation", its 15 ministries divided among nine parties, was to be sworn in on Tuesday, its main aim to stage new elections by June. Leading it was Prime Minister Bashkim Fino, a Socialist from Gjirokaster, one of the southern towns now in rebel hands.

"After consultations with all political forces we have tried to make a government for all Albanians," Bashkim told state television on Wednesday evening. "I call on Albanians in these times to think about Albania, not political forces."
Bashkim says he wants dialogue with anti-government rebels grouped in a National Committee for Public Salvation.

Fighters in the south repeated they would not give up their weapons until Berisha quit. They brought no new towns under their control but raided military bases for arms, including one near the town of Elbasan, 55 km (34 miles) from Tirana.

In some parts of the south the rebellion visibly deteriorated into lawlessness. Armed gangs roamed at will through rebel-held towns, robbing motorists, terrorising women, shooting at travellers from Greece and ignoring warnings of stern punishment issued by insurgent "defence councils".
In the capital, eyewitnesses reported groups of men had entered the military academy and removed small arms and state television reported a raid on a suburban arms depot.

The captain of a Greek Olympic Airways aircraft said he aborted a landing at Tirana airport after failing to get in touch with the control tower. There were no indications that authorities planned to close the airport.

Tension rose sharply in the capital, partly on suggestions that Berisha's supporters had seized weapons to defend him. Tirana's mayor and leaders of major political parties appeared on television to urge residents to remain calm.
More than 40 people have died in violence since January, initially sparked by the collapse of shady investment schemes which drew in the savings of hundreds of thousands.
The U.S. State Department said it was ordering 160 U.S. government employees and their dependents to leave by regular or charter flights. Another 2,000 Americans were urged to go.
A diplomatic source said orders this week by most Western countries to pull out stemmed from "logical safety criteria. They have no reflection on the country or the government".
U.S. ambassador Marisa Lino appeared on the evening news urging viewers to back the new government. "You cannot build a democracy by resorting to violence," she said in Albanian.
Television clips aired throughout the evening juxtaposed stockpiles of ammunition with children romping in a meadow with the commentary: "Brothers and sisters. No arms, no violence."

Vranitzky was due in Tirana for the second time in as many weeks to present a report on the crisis in which he urged authorities to show restraint. "Violence by any side could spark a civil conflict after of unforeseen dimension, plunging the country into a state of war," the report said.
Greek Prime Minister Costas Simitis said he was sending his foreign minister to Tirana on Friday to help defuse the crisis.

The new government emerged from days of talks between Berisha and 10 parties. Berisha reversed his opposition to including the Socialist Party, heirs to the Communists who ran Europe's most oppressive regime for 45 years until 1990.

But one party, the Democratic Alliance, withdrew after the Interior Ministry was given to Berisha's Democratic Party, accused by the opposition of rigging last May's general election in which it won all but a handful of seats.
